title: Chapter 39 – The Empty Mirror
html:
[Lin Clan – Lin Jian]

The snow begins at dusk, and by midnight it has buried the hill.

It falls the way Jian has been praying for it to fall, thick and slow and windless, in flakes as big as a thumbnail. It lies a hand deep on the terraces. It muffles the gate and the wall and the long black roofs. It swallows sound the way a pillow swallows a shout. For eleven days he has watched the sky from the granary door, and on the eleventh, at last, the clouds came down.

A flare of Qi is a lamp, Mother said, when they began to plan this. A breakthrough at the seventh stage is a very large lamp. It can be seen from a long way off by anyone who is looking. Snow is the only thing that hides a lamp.

Snow, and a wall of heat.

He sits cross-legged on a straw mat in the middle of the granary floor, with a quilt over his shoulders and his palms on his knees. The forge has been built up to a roaring red, and Hu has stacked the bellows and the crucibles and a dozen charcoal braziers in a ring around him, so that the whole building shimmers with a furnace-glow that no cultivator within a mile could separate from the glow of a working smithy. The doors are barred. The roof is mended. The two holes that the dead rogue made in the autumn have been patched with new thatch, and the thatch is thick with snow.

Mother sits against the wall by the door with her knife across her knees and her gardener's hat on the floor beside her. She has not spoken in an hour. Hu is on his bucket at the anvil. In the shadow of the anvil, Pebble lies on a folded blanket with its nose under its tail, wide awake, its scales gone a faint, anxious silver.

Jian takes a breath, and counts it. He has been counting for six weeks.

```

Qi Refining: Stage 6 (peak)
Reserve: 6.31 / 6.40
Wheel efficiency: 31%
Breath-Gathering Pills (Yellow, low): 14 taken over 41 days
Breakthrough threshold: reserve ≥ 99% of capacity, channel compression completed
Estimated success: 84%
Risk: channel damage 11% (mild), 4% (severe)
CE: 170 / 400
```

Eighty-four. He does not like the number. It is a good one, and it has been a good one for a week. But he is a man who has spent his life staring at the other sixteen percent.

Eleven mild. Four severe. He thinks of the silver scar on his right arm, the thin line of the ring. I have already paid once.

"Whenever you are ready," Mother says quietly.

"Yes."

"Do not hurry. If it does not feel right, stop. We have another winter."

"We do not."

She says nothing. The forge ticks. Pebble opens one dark eye and closes it again.

Jian closes his own, and lets go.

* * *

The Five-Gate Wheel turns.

It is a thing he has done ten thousand times, on ten thousand nights: the slow rotation of Qi through five gates, water to wood to fire to earth to metal, one gate on each breath, the same circle that he has cut into himself like a groove into a plate. But tonight it is different, because tonight he does not let it stay a circle.

Compress.

He draws the reserve inward. All six parts and thirty-one hundredths of it, every drop he has gathered in six years, a pool of warm bright water held in a bowl the size of a plum. He pulls the walls of the bowl inward, and the water rises. It presses against the channels. It is a strange, thick, humming pressure, like the sensation of holding your breath underwater, and it builds and builds.

Do not rush it.

The first gate, water, opens under the pressure like a door in a flood. Qi surges out, along the line of the arm, and the silver scar at the elbow flares with white pain. He grits his teeth. He holds the stream steady.

The second gate, wood. The pressure goes sideways and meets the second channel, and the channel stretches. He feels it. He feels the walls of it, the fine wet fibers, bend under the weight, thin and thin and thin like a bow drawn back.

Not yet. Not yet.

The third gate, fire. The heat of it runs down his spine and into his legs, and the sweat breaks out on his forehead and runs into his eyes. He does not blink. His whole mind has narrowed to a bright hard point, a single thread of attention drawn tight.

The fourth gate. Earth. Thick, slow, heavy, like pouring honey into a jar. His body is a vessel too small for what he is pouring into it.

One more.

The fifth gate. Metal.

It is the one that always troubles him, the cold bright edge of the wheel, the gate that rings. He opens it. And all at once something gives.

It is not a sound. It is a sensation, a loosening, as though a great weight he has been carrying across his shoulders for years had been quietly lifted away. The pressure goes out of the channels. The bowl of his reserve is no longer a bowl. It is a pool, wide and deep and calm, with a floor that goes down and down, and its surface is smooth as glass.

The Qi pours in.

It is not the thin, careful trickle of a pill. It is a flood, wild and bright, summoned from the air and the stone and the snow, rushing through the open gates like a river released. He feels the walls of the channels thicken. He feels the pool deepen, and deepen, and deepen. Heat blazes along his bones. A bright and terrible pressure builds behind his eyes, and he hears, from a long way off, the sound of someone moaning, and realizes it is himself.

Hold the circle.

Hold it.

Hold—

And at the center of his chest, where the black fragment lies against his heart, something wakes.

It does not pulse. It does not speak. It simply stirs, as a sleeper stirs when a hand is laid on the blanket, and a faint cold light runs outward from it along the lines of his body, tracing the gates, the channels, the whole bright web of his Qi. For an instant he sees himself from the outside, a small white figure in a ring of fire, with a pattern of silver threads laid over him like the veins in a leaf.

Then the pressure peaks, and breaks, and is gone, and he falls forward onto the mat with his forehead against the straw and a hollow roaring in his ears.

* * *

He does not know how long he lies there.

It might be minutes. It might be an hour. The forge ticks. Somebody has laid a hand on his back, and the hand is warm and shaking, and a voice says very close to his ear, in the tone of someone talking to a frightened animal, "Jian. Jian. Breathe."

He breathes.

The first breath hurts. The second less. By the fifth he can feel the straw under his cheek and the weight of the quilt on his back, and the slow warm settling of a body that has been through something and is learning how to be itself again. He lifts his head. The room is blurred. A shape kneels beside him, gray-haired and anxious. It is Hu. He is holding a cup of something, and his hand is shaking so badly that half of it has spilled.

"Drink," the old man says. "Do not talk. Drink."

He drinks. It is wine and ginger and honey and something bitter. It goes down hot and settles in his stomach like a small sun.

Behind Hu, Mother stands with her knife in her hand and her face the color of ash.

"Eight breaths," she says. "You stopped breathing for eight breaths. I counted."

"I am sorry."

"Do not be sorry." Her voice is not steady. "Tell me it worked."

He does not need the interface to tell him. He feels it. The pool in his chest is deeper than it has ever been, wide and still, with the faint cold shimmer of the new channels running through it like frost on a pond. He reaches outward with his sense, past the granary wall, into the snow and the darkness.

Six hundred paces. He feels the wall of the hill, the sleeping houses, the slow breathing of forty-one people. He feels the guards on the east gate, stamping their feet, and the tired old mule in the stable. He feels the wolves on the northern ridge, moving in a gray line through the pines, two miles off. Farther than he has ever felt anything.


"Seven," he whispers.

Hu makes a sound halfway between a laugh and a sob. Mother puts a hand over her mouth.

"In his tenth winter." Hu shakes his head slowly. "I was twenty-six when I reached the seventh. I thought I was a prodigy. Feng, at fifteen. And you, at ten, with a pseudo-root and five dim crystals, in a granary, in the snow." He wipes his eyes with the back of his wrist and does not seem to notice that he is doing it. "I am going to need more wine."

Something warm presses against Jian's side. He looks down. Pebble has crept across the mat in the dark and curled itself against his ribs, its small scaled body hot as a stone from the fire. A wave of wordless feeling comes through the thread between them: relief, and worry, and a vast, anxious, protective tenderness, like a small animal trying to stand guard over something much larger than itself.

Hurt? Hurt? You are hurt?

"Not hurt," he says. His voice is a croak. "Tired."

Tired. Good. Tired is good.

He closes his eyes. And in the quiet he hears, very faintly, Mother's voice, to nobody.

"Nine days," she says. "Nine days of nothing. He must be seen to be nothing." She stops. "Hu. It is going to snow until the morning. We have until the morning."

"Until the morning for what?" says Hu.

"For the Red Ridge riders to arrive."

* * *

They come at the third hour after dawn.

Jian is in bed. That is the story, and it is, for once, almost true. He lies in his room in the east wing, under three quilts, with a bowl of porridge on the stool beside him and Aunt Wenqing's hand on his forehead. He has a fever. He has had one for two days, everyone agrees. It is nothing dangerous, a winter chill, the kind a boy catches after carrying baskets in the rain. He is white and cold and the sweat has dried on his face. He cannot raise his own hand.

I am not pretending, he thinks, looking up at the ceiling. That is the beauty of it.

He feels them at the gate before the bell rings. Six horses, five men, one woman. The woman is the one he feels first. She is a Qi Refining ninth-stage, a peak, and she carries herself like a stone in a river, with no more movement than she needs. He knows her name. It was written in a clerk's ledger in a high gray room, three times, in a column of inquiries.

Zhao Bei. Steward of Red Ridge.

He can feel her sense go out from the horse like a hand laid across the snow. It is cold and slow and patient, and it touches the wall, the roofs, the guards. He lies very still, with his eyes closed, and does not Veil. A veil has a seam. A Foundation sense can find the seam, Mother said. And Zhao Bei does not carry only her own sense.

She has brought something with her.

He cannot see it. But he can feel it, even from here, as a faint ringing in the air, a pressure like the touch of a finger on the rim of a glass. It is bronze, and old, and it is looking.

A mirror. A relic. Profound grade, low tier.

And somebody is on the other side of it.

* * *

Father receives the steward in the main courtyard, in the snow, because there is no other place large enough, and because Lin Wenyuan has decided that a Patriarch does not hold a conference in a room with the door shut.

Jian watches it from the window of the library, with a blanket around his shoulders and Lin Hu, silent and watchful, at his elbow. He did not ask Lin Hu to help him walk. Lin Hu simply appeared in the doorway of the sickroom with a bowl of broth, and then in the passage, with an arm under his own, and has not said a word since.

Ten paces to the window, Jian thinks. Seven. Five.

"Steward Zhao," Father says in the yard below. The snow has made his breath a white plume. He wears the plain winter robe of the Patriarch and no sword. "You have come a long way. I hope the road was not too bad."

"The road was acceptable." Zhao Bei bows. She is a broad woman in her forties with a flat, calm face and iron-gray hair braided tight to her skull. Her voice is low and unhurried. "I regret the intrusion. I come on the Hall's business, and my master's. It is the winter census."

"I was not told of a census."

"It is on the Hall's schedule. The Arbiter's letter went out three weeks ago. I would be surprised if it did not reach you." A very small pause. "Perhaps in the snow."

Father says nothing. Jian, at the window, feels the shape of the lie in the air like a smell. There was no letter. She knows there was no letter. She has come with a paper that says there was.

"The Compact requires each tributary house to submit its minors for testing at the winter census," Zhao Bei goes on. "Normally at the Registry, in Willow Ford. In a hard winter, with a long road, the Hall permits a neighboring house to carry an approved instrument to the family's own door. Red Ridge has volunteered. My master thought it would be a courtesy."

"A courtesy."

"He is a considerate man." She lifts her left hand, and from the sleeve of her gray cloak she draws an object wrapped in blue cloth. She unwraps it with great care.

It is a mirror. It is round and heavy, as wide as a plate, with a rim of old green bronze and a plain, dark, polished face. There are no marks on it. There are no glyphs. It does not seem to reflect anything at all. It looks like a hole in the air.

Jian feels the cold of it from the library window. It goes through him like a draft.

Heng's.

"The Hall's approved Root-Seeking Mirror," Zhao Bei says. "Registered. I have the seal. I need only the children."

"My children," says Father, carefully, "are in the house."

"All of them? I was told there was a fever."

"One of them has a fever." Father's voice does not alter. "The rest are well. I do not believe it is wise to bring a sick child into the snow."

"A census is a census, Patriarch." Bei lifts her flat gray eyes. "If I cannot test them today, I must report it to the Arbiter. I would not like to. It would mean another visit. And you know what the Hall is like about a house that does not wish to be counted."

She is very good, Jian thinks. She is giving him no way out and not raising her voice.

His father stands motionless in the snow, with his left hand loose at his side, for the space of three breaths.

"Bring them," he says. "All of them. And Steward Zhao. I will be present at every test."

"Of course."

* * *

They line up in the snow.

Lin Hu is first. He stands stiffly, in a gray tunic that is a little too short in the sleeves, with his hands at his sides and his eyes fixed on a point just over the steward's shoulder. She holds up the mirror. He lays his palm on the cold green rim. For a moment nothing happens. Then the dark face clouds, and two colors rise out of it, red and green, steady and small, like two sparks in a lantern.

"Qi Refining, fourth stage," Zhao Bei says. "Dual root, fire and wood." She nods, and lowers the mirror, and a clerk in her party writes something on a tablet. She has not looked at Lin Hu's face once.

She has not looked at anyone's face. Jian watches from the window. She is not interested in the faces. She is waiting for one.

Lin Xiu, eight, Wenshi's daughter. First stage, wood. A cousin, a cousin, a side-branch girl. Yue is brought out last of the girls, in a thick quilted short robe that makes her look like a dumpling. She puts a small hand on the bronze and the mirror stays dark, and the steward says, in an entirely neutral voice, "No root," and moves on.

Then she looks up at the window.

It is not a glance. It is a simple, level, patient turn of the head, and her eyes find his through the glass across forty feet of snowy air. And behind her eyes, a little way back, like a face seen at the far end of a long dark tunnel, something else looks out.

Jian does not move. He does not Veil. He does not do any of the thousand small things that a hidden man does. He lets his chest rise and fall with a sick child's labored breathing. He lets his hands tremble on the blanket. He lets a thread of cold sweat run down his temple.

I am empty, he tells himself, over and over. I am a vessel with nothing in it. There is nothing to read. There is nothing to fold. Look all you like.

The pressure on the glass is very light. It moves across him slowly, like a thumb over a page. It lingers at his chest. It lingers at his hands.

Then it moves on.

"The younger son," says Zhao Bei, into the courtyard. "I would see him now."

* * *

It takes Lin Hu and Aunt Wenqing together to get him down the stairs.

He moves like an invalid, one hand on the rail, the other on Lin Hu's shoulder, with the blanket dragging at his heels. His legs are not entirely acting. He has been awake for twenty-nine hours, and the hollow in his chest where the Qi should be feels like a well that has been drained to the stones. He is dizzy. He is cold. His teeth, he realizes, are actually chattering.

Good, he thinks. Do not stop that.

At the foot of the steps, Father is waiting. He says nothing. He lays a hand on Jian's head, a quick, hard, painful pressure, and then lets him go.

Zhao Bei holds out the mirror.

It is closer than he wanted. Up close, the bronze is greener and older than he had thought, with a faint spiral running through the green like a vein through marble. The dark face gives back nothing, not his own reflection, not the courtyard, not the sky. He has the thought that it is a very long way down.

"Place your palm on the rim," Zhao Bei says.

He does.

The bronze is cold. Colder than snow. A deep, slow, dragging cold, like the touch of a river in winter, and it pulls at him, through his hand, up his arm, into his chest. It goes looking. It finds the empty pool, the new frost-bright channels, the thin pale ghost of a reserve that is nine days from full.

Eight-tenths of one part in nine, he thinks, very quietly. It is reading eight-tenths.

The mirror clouds.

Five colors rise. Faint, dim, scattered, a smear of green and red and brown and gold and blue, none of them clear, none of them bright. They hang in the dark face like a handful of dust.

"Pseudo-root," Zhao Bei says. Her voice is flat. "Five crystals, all dim. Qi Refining, second stage." She tilts her head. "You have been ill."

"A fever, ma'am," Jian says. His teeth chatter on the last word.

"You are very pale."

"I have not been able to eat."

"No. I do not suppose you have." She is looking at the mirror, not at him. But behind her eyes, a little deeper, the faint dark presence has drawn very close. It is looking at him through the bronze with an unhurried, intent, enormous patience. It rests on his face. It rests on his hand on the rim. It goes down, slowly, along the length of his arm, to the silver scar at the elbow.

It stops.

Do not look at it. Do not think about it. Be nothing.

He is a boy with a fever. He is nobody. He has been a nobody for ten years, and he has never been so good at it.

The pressure lifts.

"That is all," Zhao Bei says, and lowers the mirror. "The census is complete. The house of Lin has five minors and one rootless child. I will report it to the Hall." She wraps the bronze in its blue cloth, and tucks it back into her sleeve. "A pity about the fever. I hope it passes."

"Thank you, Steward," Father says. His voice is perfectly level.

Zhao Bei bows. She turns to her horse. Then she stops with her foot in the stirrup, and speaks, over her shoulder, as if the thought had only just occurred to her.

"My master asks me to convey one more thing," she says. "He is an old man, and he has grown lonely, up on his ridge. It has been a long winter. He has been hearing a great deal about the second son of Green Pine Hill. A quiet boy, he says. One who counts." A pause. "He would be very pleased if the child would visit him at Red Ridge, when the snow melts. For tea."

Nobody moves.

"My son is ten years old," Father says.

"My master is a hundred and eighty-six." Zhao Bei swings into the saddle. "He would like to tell the boy some stories about the hill. About the door, perhaps. About what lies at the bottom of the stairs." She gathers the reins. "He thinks the child might find them very interesting."

She does not wait for an answer. She wheels her horse and rides out under the gate, with the five men behind her, and the hooves ring on the frozen stones and are swallowed by the snow.

For a long time nobody speaks.

Then Father kneels in the slush, in the sleeve of his good winter robe, and takes Jian by both shoulders and looks at his face. His eyes are very bright. His mouth is a thin white line.

"You will not go," he says.

"No, Father."

"You will not go to Red Ridge, or to the Registry, or to the market, without me. Not for tea. Not for a stranger's stories. Not for any reason that anyone gives you." His grip tightens. "Do you understand?"

"Yes."

"Good." And then, in a voice so low that nobody else can hear: "Whatever you are, my son. Whatever it is that you have been hiding. He knows it is there."

Jian says nothing. He looks past his father's shoulder at the open gate, at the road, and at the long white slope of Red Ridge on the far side of the valley.

The snow is still coming down. It has begun to fill the hoofprints.

On the slope, a single light is burning.
